context: a letter from F. T. Buckland, which you are answering
exchanges:
lots of things to interest you. As with oysters so with fish— Salmon & trout differ according to the rivers & the rule is the bigger the river the bigger the fish. I am making a series of casts of fish, as stuffed fish are abominations— I want much to show you our fish hatchery operations at Hampton near Hampton Court   we hope this year to hatch out 100,000 fish   I hope at Galway to hatch out half a million—

I quoted your book the other day on a Salmon arbitration case   The other side wanted to make out that if the fishery had increased for seven years, it would go on increasing in same ratio for 28 years— They forgot the rules you have laid down as regards elements of self destruction in creatures— It was a question of one hundred thousand pounds so you will I think agree with me that “Practical Natural” History is important rather—

I fear I have bothered you with all this rigmarole

Yours ever | Frank Buckland

I am much obliged for your interesting letter. I had not heard that you had left the army; but I have been ill for above a year, & am still so weak that I go nowhere, & so hear no news. I shall be particularly obliged to you, if you are able to examine the feet of otter-hounds in comparison with other hounds or even with other dogs. Do not trouble yourself to send me a dead hound, I could not leave home to compare it with other hounds.

I thank you for telling me about the change in the oysters which fact I will hereafter quote on your authority; for I have met with a statement that young British oysters placed in the Meditterranean become rayed liked the shells in that sea. You must be very busy with your many pursuits, which must require indomitable energy. Some months ago we read aloud your two Vols of Miscellanea & we were all much indebted to you for much interest & amusement.

Pray believe me | yours very sincerely | Ch. Darwin
